title: When hydro is no longer enough | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Colombia's power system, historically built on cheap hydropower backed by domestic gas, is exposed on two fronts as a potentially severe El Niño approaches: dry-year climate volatility and declining domestic gas production that makes the thermal backup more expensive and import-dependent. Grupo Energía Bogotá's Alvaro Villasante argues the 2026-2027 risk window can't be closed by long-term renewables auctions alone and instead requires near-term execution on reservoir management, gas-import infrastructure, demand response, and grid investment, with Brazil's diversified, better-interconnected system as a benchmark.

themes.theme: Structural fragility of Colombia's hydro-gas model

insights.claim: Colombia's power system was historically built around abundant hydropower backed by domestic gas, producing electricity that was relatively cheap, relatively clean, and largely locally sourced.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: The legacy cost advantage of Colombian power is structurally tied to two inputs (hydro + cheap domestic gas) that are both now under pressure, which should reprice long-run generation cost assumptions for the market.
insights.quote: Colombia’s power system was built around a powerful advantage: abundant hydropower backed by domestic gas, delivering electricity that was relatively cheap, relatively clean, and largely local.

insights.claim: Colombia's power model is under pressure from two simultaneous directions: climate volatility is making dry years more dangerous for hydro output, and gas is no longer a reliable easy fallback for thermal backup generation.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: A dual-sided risk (hydro variability + gas decline) removes the natural hedge Colombia previously had between the two resources, raising the odds of price spikes or shortages in dry years.
insights.quote: Climate volatility is making dry years more dangerous, and gas is no longer the easy fallback it once was.

insights.claim: With a potentially severe El Niño approaching, the key question for Colombia's grid is no longer nameplate installed capacity but whether the system has enough firm, flexible energy to meet rising demand without price spikes or shortages.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Reframes the Colombian grid-adequacy debate from a capacity-on-paper metric to a firm/flexible-capacity metric — a lens applicable to other hydro-dependent grids facing climate risk.
insights.quote: As a potentially severe El Niño approaches, the central question is no longer just how much installed capacity the country has on paper. It is whether the system has enough firm, flexible energy to meet rising demand without driving up prices or risking shortages.

insights.claim: Hydropower remains a genuine strategic strength for Colombia but can no longer be treated as a sufficient foundation for the power system on its own.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Investors should expect Colombia's capacity-expansion mix to diversify away from hydro-only dependence, opening room for gas-import infrastructure, storage, and renewables capex.
insights.quote: Their core argument is that hydropower remains a strategic strength, but it can no longer be treated as a sufficient foundation on its own.

insights.claim: As domestic gas production declines and gas imports become more important to Colombia, the thermal backup system is becoming both more expensive and more exposed, turning a formerly stable hydro-thermal balance into a fragile equation shaped by infrastructure, timing, and security of supply.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Gas-import infrastructure buildout (regas terminals, pipelines) becomes a critical near-term investment need, not a discretionary upgrade, as domestic supply declines.
insights.quote: As gas production declines and imports become more important, the backup system is getting more expensive and more exposed, turning what used to be a relatively stable balance between hydro and thermal generation into a more fragile equation shaped by infrastructure, timing, and security of supply.

themes.theme: Near-term risk window (2026-2027) and response priorities

insights.claim: Long-term renewables auctions in Colombia are directionally the right policy tool but do little to solve the immediate risk window running through 2026 and 2027.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Long-dated renewables auctions should not be read by markets as a solution to Colombia's near-term (2026-2027) reliability risk; separate near-term measures are required.
insights.quote: Álvaro argues that long-term renewables auctions are directionally right, but they do little to solve an immediate risk window running through 2026 and 2027.

insights.claim: The practical near-term priorities for Colombia are to manage hydro reservoirs carefully, accelerate gas-import infrastructure buildout, and treat demand response and energy efficiency as core system tools rather than peripheral side issues.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term action checklist (reservoir management, gas-import capex, demand response/efficiency as system tools) for assessing Colombian utilities' and regulators' readiness ahead of the 2026-2027 risk window.
insights.quote: In the near term, the priorities are more practical: manage reservoirs carefully, accelerate gas-import infrastructure, and treat demand response and energy efficiency as system tools rather than side issues.

insights.claim: Brazil's more diversified generation mix and stronger transmission buildout make it easier to move power across regions and absorb volatility, offering a useful benchmark for Colombia, whose grid investment still lags.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Brazil's interconnection and generation-diversity model is the comparative benchmark investors should use to gauge how far behind Colombia's grid investment cycle remains.
insights.quote: The broader lesson comes from Brazil, where a more diversified generation mix and stronger transmission buildout have made it easier to move power across regions and absorb volatility, offering a useful contrast for a Colombian system still trying to catch up on grid investment.

themes.theme: Energy security as a development and equity issue

insights.claim: Energy security in Colombia is framed as ultimately about people: whether infrastructure reaches communities, whether electricity stays affordable, and whether reliable access is treated as a development priority rather than an abstract policy goal.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: Frames Colombian energy-security policy evaluation around affordability and last-mile access, not just aggregate MW/MWh — relevant to social-impact and development-finance investors.
insights.quote: Álvaro makes the case that energy security is ultimately about people: whether infrastructure reaches communities, whether electricity remains affordable, and whether reliable access is treated as a development priority rather than an abstract policy goal.

insights.claim: Colombia's next energy challenge will not be solved by any single technology; the outcome depends on execution speed across gas, transmission, renewables, storage, and demand-side measures before climate pressure exposes the full cost of delay.
insights.speaker: Sylvia Leyva Martinez
insights.so_what: A multi-front execution timeline (gas, transmission, renewables, storage, demand-side) is the risk checklist for Colombian power-sector investment ahead of the next El Niño stress event.
insights.quote: The takeaway is that Colombia’s next energy challenge will not be solved by one technology alone. It will be decided by how quickly the country can move from discussion to execution on gas, transmission, renewables, storage, and demand-side measures before climate pressure exposes the full cost of delay.
